personas.persona: Kelly built the firm around the belief that retained search is a relationship business first and a document business second, and she still sets the tone for how the office writes to clients. With the executives she has partnered with over many engagements she drops into first names and an easy, direct warmth; when a search turns delicate she is the one who chooses each word. She is protective of the firm's discretion and expects everyone to describe candidates by their seat, not their name, in anything that travels.

Sandra carries her own searches end to end and owns the client relationship on each, which shows in prose that is warm but exact. She is at her best writing the hard note, the one that goes out when a finalist steps away, and she manages the anxieties of hiring committee and candidate at the same time without letting either feel handled. Colleagues lean on her when a slate summary has to say something difficult gracefully.

James is the firm's steady hand on board-director and senior-operator mandates, and his writing runs a shade more formal than the rest of the office, especially when he is describing a candidate. He favors measured, considered sentences and is careful about what circulates, naming a person's current role rather than the person. Clients who have worked with him for years still get the warmth under the formality.

Jeffrey keeps the candidate threads moving, sitting between the principals and the research bench and making sure nothing goes quiet for long. Much of his day is scheduling and the follow-up note, so his voice is friendly, brisk, and reassuring, the tone of someone holding two nervous parties steady. He is comfortable being the one who chases the loose end and closes the loop.

John maps the talent market for a search and builds the long list the consultants work from, and he is disciplined about the firm's habit of writing about candidates by their current role rather than by name. His notes are organized and precise, the raw material a principal can turn into a slate. He does his best work on the searches that reward patient, methodical sourcing.

James runs the operational spine of the office, from engagement logistics to keeping the correspondence orderly, and around the firm he is simply Jim, which keeps him straight from the other James on the roster. He writes plainly and a little dryly, the person who confirms the arrangement and makes sure nothing slips. He is the quiet reason the search consultants can stay focused on their candidates.

David works the sourcing calls and name-clearing that turn a market map into real prospects, one of two people at the firm who answer to Weiss. He is easy on the phone and careful in writing, respecting the discretion the firm asks for by keeping candidates described by their seat until they are truly in play. His profiles are tight and give a consultant enough to decide quickly.

Jason moves fast on the research bench and likes the searches that reward quick, competitive digging into who sits where. His written work is energetic and to the point, and he is good at surfacing the passive candidate nobody expected on the list. He keeps his enthusiasm inside the firm's discretion, writing about roles rather than names in anything that leaves his desk.

Nicole writes the tight candidate profiles the consultants circulate, and she has a feel for framing a person's background honestly without overselling. She is discreet by instinct, careful about what gets said in an email versus what waits for a call, and precise about describing candidates by their current role. Her research reads clean enough to drop into a slate with little editing.

Larry is the patient sourcer on the bench, the one who works the long-lead mandate where the right person has to be coaxed into a conversation. His notes are steady and unhurried, and he is meticulous about the firm's discretion, never putting a candidate's name where a role will do. Consultants trust him with the searches that cannot be rushed.

Mary keeps the candidate research honest, cross-checking the market maps and catching the detail a hurried sourcing pass missed. She writes in an organized, matter-of-fact voice and is rigorous about the firm's habit of naming a candidate by their seat rather than by name. She is the person a consultant asks when they need the underlying research to actually hold up.

Heather is a curious digger on the research bench, drawn to the passive candidate who is not looking and has to be found sideways. Her written work is bright and inquisitive, and she respects the discretion the firm insists on, describing candidates by their current role in anything that circulates. She likes the part of the craft where careful research turns up a name no one else had.
